items.abstract: <jats:p>The drift or the mean-reversion level of short-rate models under jump-diffusion is derived to fit the initial term-structure of zero-coupon bond. In particular, the drift is obtained for Hull-White and Cox-Ingersoll-Ross short-rate models. The purpose of obtaining the drift is for the Monte-Carlo simulations for pricing exotic equity options under stochastic interest rates and exotic interest rate derivatives. The theoretical expressions for the drift are verified by Monte-Carlo simulations of the short-rate and bond paths, and show that the expectation of the discounted entities reproduce the initial zero-coupon bond term-structure. For the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model the drift is obtained by a numerical computation of a second-order ordinary differential equation using a perturbation method. The correctness of this method is verified by the Monte-Carlo results. Further, the bond partial differential equation (PDE) for the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross jump-diffusion short-rate model is also solved numerically and the results reproduce the initial zero-coupon bond term-structure. This bond PDE computation verifies the self-consistency of the drift computation, and also validates the numerical boundary conditions used in the finite-difference computations of this final-value problem.  Similar results are presented from the finite-difference computation of the Hull-White PDE also.</jats:p>
title: Calibrating Drift of Short-Rate Models with Jump-Diffusion

items.abstract: <jats:p>One of the contentious issues regarding the post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) is whether the abnormal stock return is driven by investors’ delayed reaction to earnings information or by unexpected information shocks subsequent to earnings announcement. In this paper, we disentangle unexpected large changes in stock prices, known as jumps, from total stock returns.  Although on average jump occurs only once per firm quarter, it accounts for up to 40% of the return differential between top and bottom SUE deciles. This is evidence that a significant part of PAED is driven by unexpected information shocks.  Nevertheless, the drift component still explains at least 50% of the variation of anomalous PEAD returns. The findings suggest that PEAD cannot be entirely attributed to investors’ delayed reaction to earnings information, but neither can the hypothesis be ruled out. In particular, we find that delayed reaction is more pronounced following positive earnings surprises.</jats:p>
title: Drift or Jump: What Drives Post-Earnings Announcement Stock Returns?

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>For one-dimensional jump-drift and jump-diffusion processes converging toward some steady state, the large deviations of a long dynamical trajectory are described from two perspectives. Firstly, the joint probability of the empirical time-averaged density, of the empirical time-averaged current and of the empirical time-averaged jump-flow are studied via the large deviations at level 2.5. Secondly, the joint probability of the empirical jumps and of the empirical excursions between consecutive jumps are analyzed via the large deviations at level 2.5 for the alternate Markov chain that governs the series of all the jump events of a long trajectory. These two general frameworks are then applied to three examples of positive jump-drift processes without diffusion, and to two examples of jump-diffusion processes, in order to illustrate various simplifications that may occur in rate functions and in contraction procedures.</jats:p>
title: Jump-drift and jump-diffusion processes: large deviations for the density, the current and the jump-flow and for the excursions between jumps

items.abstract: <jats:p>We show the convergence of an online stochastic gradient descent estimator to obtain the drift parameter of a continuous-time jump-diffusion process. The stochastic gradient descent follows a stochastic path in the gradient direction of a function to find a minimum, which in our case determines the estimate of the unknown drift parameter. We decompose the deviation of the stochastic descent direction from the deterministic descent direction into four terms: the weak solution of the non-local Poisson equation, a Riemann integral, a stochastic integral, and a covariation term. This decomposition is employed to prove the convergence of the online estimator and we use simulations to illustrate the performance of the online estimator.</jats:p>
title: Online drift estimation for jump-diffusion processes

                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">Le sujet de la thèse est l’estimation paramétrique et non-paramétrique dans des modèles de processus à sauts. La thèse est constituée de 3 parties qui regroupent 4 travaux. La première partie, qui est composée de deux chapitres, traite de l'estimation des paramètres de dérive et volatilité par des méthodes de contraste depuis des observations discrètes, avec pour objectif principal de minimiser les conditions sur le pas d'observation, afin que celui ci puisse par exemple aller arbitrairement lentement vers 0. La seconde partie de la thèse concerne des développements asymptotiques, et correction de biais, pour l'estimation de la volatilité intégrée. La troisième partie de la thèse, concerne l'estimation adaptative de la mesure stationnaire pour des processus à saut.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>In this paper, we study a multi-asset periodic investment problem under capital injections, stochastic drift, jump risk, cash-flow costs, and weighted intertemporal downside-risk constraints. Unlike a selffinancing portfolio, a periodic investment account is affected by the timing of capital injections, the net investable amount, and the remaining investment horizon of each injected cash flow. We model risky assets by a multi-asset Merton jump-diffusion process with stochastic drift, where Brownian motions describe continuous market fluctuations, common jumps capture systematic shocks, and idiosyncratic jumps capture asset-specific shocks. Cash-flow costs account for the gap between gross capital injections and net investable cash flows, while the traditional terminal downside-risk constraint is extended to a weighted intertemporal form. To handle the distributional and tail-risk difficulties caused by the accumulation of dependent wealth components, we use a comonotonic approximation and reformulate the downside-risk constraint through the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) of the corresponding loss variable. Compared with the existing stochastic-drift periodic investment framework, we derive a sharper CVaR upper bound for the stochastic drift component by refining the treatment of the positive-part expectation. This yields a less conservative risk amplification coefficient. We then derive a fractional Kelly strategy within the constant mix strategy class and further develop a rolling-horizon fractional Kelly strategy, in which portfolio allocations are updated using rolling parameter estimates and current account wealth. We conduct numerical experiments using daily data for five representative A-share stocks. The model comparison shows that the proposed return model, which incorporates stochastic drift together with systematic and idiosyncratic jump risks, achieves better empirical fit than benchmark models that omit either stochastic drift or jump risk, as measured by the AIC and BIC criteria. Strategy comparisons under realized price paths show that the rolling-horizon strategy achieves higher terminal wealth and a higher return per unit of gross risky exposure, although it also involves larger risky exposure and higher turnover. Sensitivity analyses further indicate that the monitoring frequency, cash-flow costs, rebalancing costs, the safety-level coefficient, the tail probability, and the specification of the risk amplification coefficient all affect portfolio exposure and wealth performance. These results suggest that the proposed framework provides a flexible approach to dynamic asset allocation under long-term capital injections and downside-risk control.</jats:p>
title: Periodic Investment under Capital Injections with Stochastic Drift and Multi-Asset Jump Risk

items.abstract: <jats:p>Consider a random walker on the nonnegative lattice, moving in continuous time, whose positive transition intensity is proportional to the time the walker spends at the origin. In this way, the walker is a jump process with a stochastic and adapted jump intensity. We show that, upon Brownian scaling, the sequence of such processes converges to Brownian motion with inert drift (BMID). BMID was introduced by Frank Knight in 2001 and generalized by White in 2007. This confirms a conjecture of Burdzy and White in 2008 in the one-dimensional setting.</jats:p>
title: Convergence of jump processes with stochastic intensity to Brownian motion with inert drift

items.abstract: <jats:p>Stationary drift vortices in plasmas are studied analytically. It is demonstrated how to obtain explicit monopole vortex solutions of this kind. They contain a core region with closed streamlines, and have an arbitrary radial profile. A simple expression giving the propagation velocity of the vortices is obtained, and it is found that for the vortices to be stationary, the velocity should not be close to the phase velocity of linear waves. This requires a large amplitude.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Concept drift represents a fundamental challenge in intrusion detection systems, as the non-stationary nature of network environments causes continuous shifts in data distributions that progressively compromise model performance. Existing approaches typically detect concept drift through distribution-based statistics and react using fixed model update mechanisms, without explicitly leveraging the structural evolution of the data stream to guide adaptive model expansion. In this work, we propose a drift-aware adaptive framework where the structural evolution of data streams on the Grassmann manifold guides the controlled expansion of a dynamic Mixture-of-Experts architecture. Incoming data windows are represented as subspaces whose temporal evolution is modeled using Grassmannian geometry. Drift is quantified through distances between consecutive subspaces, providing a principled measure of geometric change in the latent feature space. Rather than relying on uniform adaptation strategies, the proposed framework leverages the magnitude of detected drift to guide selective model expansion. When significant geometric deviations are identified, new experts based on Hoeffding Tree classifiers are instantiated to capture emerging subspace structures, while previously learned experts are retained to preserve historical knowledge, mitigate catastrophic forgetting, and maintain a balance between stability and plasticity under non-stationary conditions. Experimental results on the NSL-KDD, CIDDS-001, and IoTID20 intrusion detection benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed approach enhances classification performance under concept drift, achieving recall rates above 98.63%, false alarm rates below 5.45%, and throughput of up to 9551.72 instances per second, supporting near real-time intrusion detection.</jats:p>
